[
1
]  The plaintiff claims damages alleging
he was libeled by an article written in the defendant's newspaper.  The
published article appeared in the Globe and Mail on October 22, 1994, as
follows:

BENEVOLENCE

CHARITABLE
DONATIONS BEGIN AT HOME AND END UP HEAVEN   KNOWS WHERE

by Robert Matas

The Globe and Mail

HOW JUST ABOUT ANY CANADIAN CAN BECOME A
BIT OF A FREELANCER IN    FOREIGN POLICY - WITH THE GOVERNMENT'S BLESSING

As
Barry Goodhead watched television last summer in his comfortable 15th‑floor
apartment in Vancouver, Rwandan refugee families seemed to limp right out of
the screen and into his living room.  There they stood in their wretchedness.
The pain in the eyes of the starving children was especially hard to ignore.
Ethiopia, Somalia, Bosnia and now another human calamity in Rwanda.  This time,
Mr. Goodhead promised himself, this time he was going to do something.

Raising
money for the Red Cross, the United Nations Children's Fund or any other
charity did not interest him because he wasn't sure how they used their funds.
Instead, Mr. Goodhead, a 51-year‑old former construction worker who was
housebound because of an old leg injury, decided to collect money himself and
use it to help the dying youngsters of the East African country.  Within a
week, the federal government had given him permission to solicit funds and
provide tax receipts on behalf of his new charity, the Canadian Society for the
Children of

Rwanda.
As soon as he registered the name with the provincial government, he was in
business.

Just
like that, Mr. Goodhead, good‑hearted and well intentioned but with no
experience in fund raising or administering a charity, was handed a licence to
tap into government revenue and spend an unlimited amount of it on activities
of his own choosing in a foreign country.

If
anyone had bothered at the outset to ask specific questions about the charity,
Mr. Goodhead probably could not have answered.  No one asked how he intended to
deliver on his good intentions or how his efforts fit into Canada's publicly
debated policy on Rwanda or into the intricate web of global politics and Third
World assistance programs.

And
no one was going to require Mr. Goodhead to account for how all the money was
spent.  To qualify for registration, a group must state that its activities
would benefit the public either through the relief of poverty, advancement of
religion or education, or by other purposes such as disaster relief.  After
setting up operations, the charity is required to file an annual report in which
it is expected to describe its programs and how much money was spent.  However
a sampling of annual reports filed with Revenue Canada show that charities, in
fact, provide extremely sparse details about their activities.

Shortly
after receiving federal approval to raise funds, Mr. Goodhead had not decided
how the money would be spent.  He thought of building a school for the
children.  Six weeks later, he had a plan: Once he had enough money, he would
go to Africa, buy land and build something to house and school 5,000 orphans.

To
raise funds, he printed a simple orange promotional handbill, set up accounts
at neighbourhood banks (so donors could contribute where they bank) and tried
to generate publicity.  But to his dismay the local media, accustomed to the
glitzy promotions of well-established charities, were not interested.  By this
week, almost three months after he had begun to organize the charity, he had
collected only $40.

Barry
Goodhead's Children of Rwanda is one of 71,000 charities blessed by the
Canadian government and, although his efforts may be above reproach, his
charity raises questions about accountability and integrity ‑
accountability for money raised through the use of the public treasury and the
integrity of honouring Canada's interests abroad.

Mr.
Goodhead demonstrated how just about any Canadian can become a bit of a
freelancer in foreign policy ‑ with the government's blessing.  If he had
wanted, he could have given his Canadian dollars for humanitarian aid to the
most vicious murderers in Rwanda.  Canada's imprimatur has been given to a host
of similar organizations whose major activities are conducted outside the
country and beyond the view of most taxpayers.

[Please
see
CLAIMS - D2
]

CLAIMS FOR DONATIONS LAST YEAR REDUCED
TAX

REVENUES BY $800-MILLION

• From Page D1

The plight of Rwandan children moved Canadians to dig into their
pockets this year.

(
RUSSEL
MONK/The Globe and Mail
)

These
good works come at a considerable cost to Canadian taxpayers.  Charities say
they received about $8.2‑billion in personal donations last year, of
which about $1‑billion was sent overseas.  The price paid from federal
coffers comes in the form of tax credits for citizens who contribute. Many
donors do not take advantage of the tax break.

Nevertheless,
personal tax credits were claimed last year for donations of $3.2‑billion,
which reduced government revenues by $800-million.

The
government has not calculated the tax credits as a result of money sent
overseas for charitable purposes.  Revenue Canada cannot separate the amount of
money spent by charities such as the Red Cross on humanitarian aid from the
amount of money spent by charities such as the Royal Winnipeg Ballet on a
foreign tour.  However, tax credits arising from overseas spending are
substantial - one estimate puts the figure at more than $100‑million ‑
which translates into a substantial cut in revenues from the public treasury.

Rwanda
has been exceptionally good for fund‑raising organizations this year.
They were able to tap into the emotional response to live television coverage
of a desperate people fleeing civil war and starvation. Within charity circles,
some say Rwanda was the most lucrative event for Canadian charities since
Ethiopia suffered a famine 10 years ago.

Over
the years, Revenue Canada's lengthy registry of domestic and international
charities ­amounts to an index of political hot spots and natural disasters.  A
quick look turns up Bangladesh and Indo‑China in the early seventies;
Afghanistan, Iraq and Peru in the eighties; Bosnia and Rwanda in the nineties.
Canadian charities provided earthquake relief for Italy in 1976 and again in
1980, and hurricane relief for Jamaica in 1988.  Action‑Haiti was
registered in September, 1993, a year before United States troops arrived on
Haiti's shores.  The Palestinian Foundation was registered as a charity shortly
after the famous Yassar Arafat‑Itzhak Rabin handshake on the White House
lawn last fall.

The
Revenue Canada list also includes charities involved in more controversial
activities.  Nine years ago, Babbar Khalsa, a militant Indian separatist group,
was implicated in the Air India bombing over the Atlantic Ocean that killed 329
people, including 279 Canadians.  The sect's leader, Canadian Talwinder Singh
Parmar, who died last year under suspicious circumstances, had claimed he was
the prime suspect in a subsequent investigation, although police made no arrests.
About the same time, external affairs minister Joe Clark advised Canadian
premiers to have nothing to do with the British Columbia‑based Babbar
Khalsa.

Notwithstanding
its tarnished reputation, the Babbar Khalsa Society applied to Ottawa in 1992 for
official recognition as a charity.  In an only‑in‑Canada twist, the
application was approved, enabling supporters to reduce their taxes by donating
to Babbar Khalsa.

According
to Revenue Canada documents, its executive includes Mr. Parmar's brother Kulwaran,
Mr. Parmar's son Jaswinder and a Kamloops resident, Avtar Singh Narwal, who is
facing a criminal charge of uttering a threat in connection with the affairs of
a local Sikh temple.  The group's annual report says the society
"promotes, teaches and maintains the character of Sikhism" through
circulation of publications and church gatherings.  Services are held either at
members' homes or at the temple.  Nothing is stated in the report about
activities outside the country, except to say that they were not carried out by
the charity's employees.  Official receipts were issued last year for $5,027.

For
the families of those who were killed in the Air India explosion, what does
this mean?  Put bluntly, the federal government in effect is offering an incentive
to Canadians to contribute to the organization created by the prime suspect of
the bloodiest terrorist airplane bombing in aviation history.

From
India to Ireland, Canadian taxpayers ‑ without even knowing it ‑
step fearlessly into some of the world's most enduring conflicts.  The Toronto‑based
Ireland Fund of Canada, which bills itself as a non-political, non‑partisan
organization, has its own vision of Northern Ireland.  Strengthened by $2.3‑million
in donations in the past five years, the fund aims to be a voice of moderation
in a country of violent extremes, where 3,168 people have been killed in the
past 25 years.

One
of its proudest achievements is its contribution to integrated Protestant-Roman
Catholic schools in Northern Ireland ‑ even though such a system is
neither supported nor approved of by the majority of the Irish population.  To
many Canadians, integrated schools in Ireland may seem like a sensible idea.
However, a moment's contemplation suggests Ottawa should not be giving tax incentives
to spur the fund on.  How would Quebec react, for example, if a British group
began raising money to support English-language education in the province?

Canadians
with ties to the former Yugoslavia have also used the stamp of government
approval to raise funds for their forays into foreign affairs.  The World
Movement for Peace in Bosnia qualified as a tax deductible charity in November,
1993.  William Vander Zalm, co‑chair of the charity and a former British
Columbia premier ‑ his wife Lillian is of Croatian descent ‑ says
the charity was initially created to raise awareness in Canada of Bosnia's
problems.  Its purpose shifted from giving out information to providing
assistance, and the group began helping Bosnians who had fled to Canada.  As
the activists were drawn into the lives of the refugees, the charity started to
raise money for Bosnians in their war‑torn homeland to buy medical
supplies and clothing.

The
World Movement makes its own decisions about where to send its money.  Mr.
Vander Zalm says the organization does not have a magic wand to wipe away a
history of hatred, "but every bit helps and if nobody cared, if nobody
became involved, if everybody walked away from it, I suppose [the hostilities]
would go on forever."

Who
can argue with peace in Bosnia?  But what have the views of the World Movement
for Peace got to do with tax deductions?  The government cannot point to a
return from its tax incentives, especially since it is not even monitoring the
World Movement closely.

Cliff
Serwa, a British Columbia politician who was part of a recent Jewish National
Fund campaign to raise money for projects in Israel, suggests that the
government subsidy it receives through tax breaks is just "seed
money." The fund has been involved in land reclamation since 1901 and
planted more than 200 million trees in the desert.  The Canadian section of the
fund issued official tax receipts in 1992 for $7.1‑million.  After
administration and fund‑raising costs, it had $4.9 million to spend on
overseas projects.

Without
tax breaks, governments would be called upon to help more agencies, which would
lead to a horrendous increase in taxes and a bureaucratic mind‑set.
Raising money for the Jewish National Fund is "not a job, it's a cause,
and volunteers approach it with a great deal of zeal.  For government
employees, it would be just a job," Mr. Serwa says.

But
would the government really be under pressure to undertake more projects in
Israel if the JNF did not receive tax breaks?

The
return to the Canadian taxpayer from dollars sent abroad is amorphous,
difficult to measure.  Despite a helping hand from Revenue Canada, charities
are under no compunction to further the official position of the Canadian
government on foreign affairs.

Furthermore,
many charities are so compelling in their appeal that they would likely receive
contributions regardless of tax deductibility.  Research in this area has
backed up anecdotal evidence.  Most contributors will donate even without
receiving a tax receipt.   The tax credits, and loss of government revenue, are
not necessary for a charity to raise money.

Mississauga-based
World Vision, which regularly appeals for money on television with pictures of
starving children in developing countries, is one of the most successful
international fund-raising charities in Canada.  About 170,000 Canadians
regularly send $27 each month to World Vision Canada to feed 190,000 children
in different parts of the world.  About 70,000 teen-agers participate in its
fund-raising campaign, raising $2-million for the charity.  Another 80,000
Canadians respond to direct appeals in the media or through the mail.

The
charity expects to collect $80-million in private donations this year, which
could cost the government at least $15-million in reduced tax payments.
Parliament gives up the money without even a brief glance at the charity's
overseas activities.

Philip
Maher, a spokesman for World Vision Canada, says many people see their
contribution to the charity as an expression of support for more foreign aid
from Canada.  The federal government is giving $2.7-billion in aid this year, a
drop from $2.9-billion last year.  Despite a commitment by both the former
Conservative government and the current Liberal administration to increase
assistance to developing countries, foreign aid has been heading in the
opposite direction.

"The
bottom line is the government has a political agenda.  That's not evil, that's
democracy and they've got to listen to the people,"  Mr. Maher says.
World Vision Canada, however, can spend its money any way it wants, including
on things the government may be unwilling to fund, he adds.

Precisely
the problem.  Charities are collecting money with the assistance of a tax break
to undertake projects that in some instances the government would not undertake
itself.

Meanwhile,
the charities are aware of the research that shows tax credits do not make a
big difference to Canadians' donations.  "Either you believe in [a cause]
or you don't," says Quebec businessman Tom Nacos.  Mr. Nacos was honoured
last spring at a Jewish National Fund dinner in Montreal that raised $750,000
for a reservoir in Israel to hold water from the Jordan River.  Tax receipts
have nothing to do with charity, he says.  "I believe if you're going to
be a donor, I don't think the tax should be the reason you do it."

And
most Canadians seem to agree with Mr. Nacos.  Strange, then, that Ottawa
happily forgoes some close to a billion each year.

[
2
]  The story concerning Mr. Goodhead
appeared on the front page of the Focus section of the newspaper and the
balance of the article appeared on page 2 of the same section.  Mr. Goodhead
says that a number of statements in the article were untrue and that there was
malice behind the article.  Mr. Goodhead says that his father was a wealthy and
powerful person in Ontario who owned a disposal dump that was causing pollution
and injury to children.  He alleges that the Globe and Mail wrote a number of
articles about his father in the 1980s and that this article about the
plaintiff, written by Mr. Matas,     was motivated by some form of
mala
fides
against the Goodhead name.  Mr. Matas gave evidence and said he had
never heard of Mr. Goodhead's father, had never seen any articles about the
Goodhead family and knew nothing about the disposal dump in Ontario.

[
3
]  I accept Mr. Matas' evidence.  There is
no evidence from which I can conclude that he is not telling the truth and I
conclude that the article that he wrote about the plaintiff in this case was
done in good faith and without malice.

[
4
]  I find that the article does not libel
the plaintiff, Barry Goodhead.  The article describes Mr. Goodhead as
"...good-hearted and well intentioned but with no experience in fund
raising or administering a charity,...."  I can find no misstatements of
fact in the article which would lower Mr. Goodhead's reputation in the eyes of
right-thinking people.

[
5
]  Mr. Goodhead complained about a number
of misstatements of fact in the article.  For example, the article said that he
lived on the 15th floor of an apartment whereas he, in fact, lived on the 11th
floor.  Although this is a misstatement of fact, it is not libelous.

[
6
]  He also complained that the entire
first nine paragraphs of the article referred to Mr. Goodhead personally,
implying that this was his charity and that he had the power to administer it
as he saw fit.  He said that the board of directors consisted of his wife, his
son, his daughter and his mother-in-law and no cheques could be written without
the signature of another person, whereas the inference in the article is that
he could act alone.

[
7
]  In my view, the description of Mr.
Goodhead as being a person behind the charity with the power to make decisions
accurately reflects the situation.  His son was a minor and probably not
legally authorized to sign the society incorporation documents.  His
mother-in-law's signature purports to appear on the documents but she never did
sign them in fact, and they were signed on her behalf.  Mr. Goodhead's son did
not want to hand out leaflets soliciting funds for the charity even though he
did so, and his daughter refused to do it.  Mr. Goodhead said that the charity
was his idea because he felt guilt that his father was a very wealthy man in
Ontario who owned a polluting dump.

[
8
]  Mr. Goodhead was the spokesperson for
the charity and he was the only person who gave evidence.  I think the article
accurately reflects Mr. Goodhead as being the spearhead and spokesperson for
the charity and it is not misleading.  However, even if the article were
misleading on this point, in that Mr. Goodhead required a resolution of the
board of directors to make decisions, the description of him is not libelous in
the sense that it would lower his reputation in the community.

[
9
]  Mr. Goodhead next complained that the
statement, "And no one was going to require Mr. Goodhead to account for
how all the money was spent..." was libelous because the society would
have to file tax returns.  In my view, the article accurately states the
situation.  From a practical point of view, charities registered in Canada
collect money and at taxpayers' expense send funds to foreign countries with no
accounting as to how the monies are spent.  Indeed, in this very case, the
charity in which Mr. Goodhead is involved collected $50, sent it to the Red
Cross, and has not been required to account for how the monies were disbursed.
In any event, if there is a libel in this statement it is not of Mr. Goodhead
but is a comment on the government system which allows the collection of funds
for charities.

[
10
] Mr. Goodhead also complained that the
charity was referred to as "The Canadian Society for the Children of
Rwanda" when in fact the proper name of the society was "For the
Children of Rwanda (In Trust)."  In fact, the registration for federal tax
purposes was called "For the Children of Rwanda (In Trust)."
However, that name was unacceptable to the provincial authorities for
registration under the
Societies Act
and the
plaintiff selected another name which was "The Canadian Society for the
Children of Rwanda."

[
11
] In his article, Mr. Matas referred to
"The Canadian Society for the Children of Rwanda" which he took from
a flier that was distributed by the plaintiff.  It is perfectly reasonable that
Mr. Matas would have referred to that name since it is the name under which the
plaintiff was collecting funds.  In any event, even if he had got the name
wrong it did not libel Mr. Goodhead.

[
12
] Mr. Goodhead also complained that the
statement, "If he had wanted, he could have given his Canadian dollars for
humanitarian aid to the most vicious murderers in Rwanda" libeled him.
Mr. Goodhead was furious about this statement and found it extremely
offensive.  I find that this statement is a true statement of fact, that is,
Mr. Goodhead does have the right to send his money where he chooses, even to
murderers in Rwanda.  There is no suggestion in the article that Mr. Goodhead
would do that; only that the laws as they are in Canada would permit him to do
it.  Earlier in the article Mr. Matas describes Mr. Goodhead's efforts as being
above reproach.

[
13
] Looking at the article as a whole, it
is clearly an article about government policy and how Canadian tax dollars are
being sent all over the world at the instance of anyone who decides to create a
charity.  There is no accountability for those monies and we do not know how
they are being spent in foreign countries.  It is true that people without
experience can get into the charity business and it appears from the evidence
in Mr. Matas' article that there are a number of questionable charities.

[
14
] I conclude that Mr. Matas' article was
a thoughtful and well researched piece of investigative journalism.  The story
about Mr. Goodhead was simply an example of how easy it is for anyone to get
into the charity business.

[
15
] I conclude that there is nothing in the
article that would lower Mr. Goodhead's reputation in the eyes of right-thinking
people and that the article does not libel Mr. Goodhead.  I therefore dismiss
this action.

"F.
Maczko J."

F.
MACZKO J.
